## Results

### Data summary

After quality control filtering, [N_valid] valid observation-days across
[N_years] calendar years (1986--2025) were available for analysis. The
overall circular mean peak hour was [mean_hour]:00 local time
(circular~SD~ = [circ_std]~h~), confirming that the daily maximum at
{\'E}pinal typically occurs in the mid-afternoon, consistent with
boundary-layer heating dynamics.

### Primary trend estimate

The von Mises circular regression yielded a slope of
[beta]~h/decade~ (95~\% bootstrap CI: [ci_lower], [ci_upper];
$\kappa$ = [kappa]). This [indicates a shift toward later/earlier
peak timing / suggests no detectable shift over the study period].

Figure~\ref{fig-wrapped-scatter} shows the daily peak-hour observations
with the fitted von Mises trend line and 95~\% confidence band. The
hexagonal binning reveals the dominant concentration of peak hours in
the 14:00--18:00 window (approximately [pct]~\% of observations), with
the broad spread reflecting meteorological day-to-day variability.

![Daily peak-hour observations (hexbin density) with von Mises

### Sensitivity analyses

All eight pre-registered sensitivity variants produced results
consistent with the primary estimate (Table~\ref{tbl-sensitivity}),
indicating that the trend is not driven by any single methodological
choice.

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95~\% CI | n~obs |
|---------|--------------------|----------|-------|
| Primary (earliest tie) | [beta_p] | [ci_p_l, ci_p_u] | [n_p] |
| Latest tie | [beta_l] | [ci_l_l, ci_l_u] | [n_l] |
| Min years = 20 | [beta_y] | [ci_y_l, ci_y_u] | [n_y] |
| MAD threshold = 3.0 | [beta_m] | [ci_m_l, ci_m_u] | [n_m] |
| Exclude post-2000 | [beta_e] | [ci_e_l, ci_e_u] | [n_e] |
| 3-hour subsampling | [beta_3h] | [ci_3h_l, ci_3h_u] | [n_3h] |
| 6-hour subsampling | [beta_6h] | [ci_6h_l, ci_6h_u] | [n_6h] |
| Min amplitude 1.0~°C | [beta_a1] | [ci_a1_l, ci_a1_u] | [n_a1] |
| Min amplitude 3.0~°C | [beta_a3] | [ci_a3_l, ci_a3_u] | [n_a3] |
: Summary of primary and sensitivity analysis results.
  $\beta$ is in hours per decade; CI bounds are 2.5th and 97.5th
  bootstrap percentiles. {#tbl-sensitivity}

Figure~\ref{fig-rose-diagram} compares the circular distribution of

### Seasonal patterns

The seasonal sub-analyses (Table~\ref{tbl-seasonal}) [revealed
heterogeneous trends across seasons / were broadly consistent with the
annual result]. [Spring/summer/autumn/winter] showed the largest
estimated shift at [beta_season]~h/decade~, while
[spring/summer/autumn/winter] showed [no detectable trend / the weakest
signal].

| Season | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95~\% CI | n~obs |
|--------|--------------------|----------|-------|
| Spring (MAM) | [beta_sp] | [ci_sp_l, ci_sp_u] | [n_sp] |
| Summer (JJA) | [beta_su] | [ci_su_l, ci_su_u] | [n_su] |
| Autumn (SON) | [beta_au] | [ci_au_l, ci_au_u] | [n_au] |
| Winter (DJF) | [beta_wi] | [ci_wi_l, ci_wi_u] | [n_wi] |
: Seasonal von Mises regression results. CI bounds are 2.5th and 97.5th
  bootstrap percentiles. {#tbl-seasonal}

Figure~\ref{fig-seasonal} presents the per-season trend panels.
Note that the exploratory nature of these analyses (no multiple-testing
correction) warrants cautious interpretation.

![Seasonal von Mises regression trends. Each panel shows hexbin density
  of daily peak hours and the fitted trend line with 95~\% CI band.
  ](results/figures/seasonal_trend.pdf){#fig-seasonal}

### Supplementary analyses

Temperature-weighted von Mises regression (weighting each day by its
diurnal amplitude) produced a consistent estimate of
[beta_w]~h/decade~, confirming that the trend is not driven by days
with poorly defined peaks. The circular--linear rank correlation
(Mardia 1976) yielded $\rho_c$ = [rho_c] ([p-value = / p~{\textless}~]
0.05), corroborating the MLE-based result.
